claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr in the as-cast state.
As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr has high room-temperature strength.
As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr has high elevated-temperature strength.
A portion of Hf should be replaced by additional Ti.
Hf is the heavier, higher-density component relative to Ti.
Replacing Hf with Ti will decrease the alloy's mass density.
An appropriate Hf-to-Ti substitution level can retain phase stability.
The modified alloy will remain a single-phase solid solution.
The modified alloy will retain severe lattice distortion.
Solid-solution strengthening is relevant to the mechanical behavior of the studied Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy family, which includes HfMoTaTiZr.
Retaining lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening will sustain the modified alloy's mechanical properties.
Ti addition in similar alloy modifications decreases density while promoting solid-solution strengthening and lattice distortion.
The modified alloy will have a density significantly below 10.21 g/cm³.
The modified alloy will retain similar compressive strength and yield strength at room temperature relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain similar compressive ductility at room temperature relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain similar compressive strength, ductility, and yield strength near 1000 °C relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The proposed performance comparison is limited to compressive loading from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis allows an unspecified optimal substitution level, but the rejection rule says failure of one or more members of a composition series falsifies the hypothesis. A single poorly performing substitution level does not rule out another level that lowers density while preserving properties.

Failure to obtain any density reduction would contradict the hypothesis, yet the stated rejection rule only activates when an alloy first demonstrates reduced density and then loses mechanical performance.
